title: Beyond Artificial Intelligence: Vocation and the Sacred Relationship Between Physician and Patient.
desc: [The Linacre quarterly] The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine should be discussed following Pope Leo XIV's recent encyclical on AI and the need to protect human dignity in this era of advancing technology. As a result of its efficiency and accessibility to people for medical advice, AI is already starting to change healthcare. These advances may improve patient care, but medicine is about more than access to information. Medicine is a vocation motivated by the compassionate service to others, and this must be defended. Using the teachings of Antiqua et Nova and Magnifica Humanitas as a guide, this commentary discusses how Catholic bioethics can contribute to the integration of AI in clinical practice. These ethical principles can direct the proper use of AI while still upholding physicians' responsibilities to their patients. Physicians must recognize each patient's dignity and needs, which go beyond the knowledge that any algorithm can offer. Furthermore, the recommendations that these AI systems provide are only as strong as the information available to them, emphasizing the continued importance of the physician's clinical judgment. As we continue to monitor the emergence and growth of AI, the Church serves as a reminder to us that AI should support physicians' clinical judgment while preserving the sacred relationship of trust between physician and patient.

title: Multi-center Prospective Validation of Real-Time AI-EGGIM System
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Qilu Hospital of Shandong University; conditions: Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 540; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM) is a precancerous condition associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer. The endoscopic grading of gastric intestinal metaplasia (EGGIM) score evaluates the extent of GIM across five standard gastric regions. The investigators developed a real-time artificial intelligence-assisted EGGIM (AI-EGGIM) system that automatically assigns an intestinal metaplasia grade to each region and calculates a total EGGIM score. This prospective multi-center validation study will consecutively enroll patients undergoing upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. The AI-EGGIM system will generate real-time grades for the five standard gastric regions. Regardless of endoscopic appearance or AI output, every patient will undergo five mapping biopsies, with one biopsy obtained from each standard region. Histopathological operative link on gastric intestinal metaplasia (OLGIM) staging will serve as the reference standard. The primary objective is to estimate the performance of an AI-EGGIM score ≥ 5 for identifying patients at high risk of gastric cancer.

title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
desc: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.

title: A decision-only model as a low-cost judge of medical AI answers
desc: BackgroundTesting and deploying medical AI systems at scale already results in more outputs than clinicians can review, and the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges is growing rapidly. Decision-only models, cheap and fast models that return structured probabilities rather than text, offer a potentially scalable option for that goal. MethodsIn an OSF pre-registered evaluation, we tested TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as a judge on tasks from five validated clinical benchmarks: rubric grading (HealthBench), planted clinical errors (When Rubrics Fail), risk in AI-written clinical documents (MedVAL), counseling ratings and failures (CounselBench) and physicians preferences between answers (Real-POCQi). Comparators were expert raters agreement with each other, OpenAI Decisions, GPT-6 Luna, a proposed hybrid team combining decision models and a cheap LLM and, as frontier comparators, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label. ResultsThe test comprised 25,091 units and 213,913 model calls. Jevs agreement with expert labels averaged 64.7% over six tasks. On 3,614 matched units it averaged 66.1%, against 65.0% for Opus and 60.7% for Sol, and it was non-inferior to both on four of six tasks. Jev judged the whole pool in 17 minutes for US$1.46; per judgment, it cost 1/34 of Sols price and 1/152 of Opuss. A preset cutoff held its false-alarm rate on fresh planted-error answers, and in simulation, reviewing Jevs least-sure answers first found 1.4 times the errors of a random audit. Still, omissions were hard for both: at the same false-alarm rate, Jev missed 55.6% of planted omissions and Opus 48.1%, and Opus caught 8.8 points more planted errors overall. ConclusionsAcross more than 200,000 model calls, a decision-only model was non-inferior to two frontier judges on most tasks at a small fraction of their cost and time, while reporting how sure it was of every call. With local cutoffs and expert oversight of omissions and clinical documents, judging every output of a deployed medical AI system becomes more affordable.

title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
desc: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

title: Artificial intelligence in dialysis.
source: PubMed · Current opinion in nephrology and hypertension
desc: [Current opinion in nephrology and hypertension] Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in dialysis have matured beyond the initial phase of algorithm development. Recent work has shifted toward clinical implementation, evaluation, and governance. During the past year, the first randomized trial of AI-guided dosing in maintenance hemodialysis has been published, a meta-analysis of technology-guided dry-weight adjustment has appeared, and the first professional society framework for the responsible use of AI in kidney care has been released. The Anemia Control Model is now supported by hospitalization outcomes and cost-effectiveness analyses. A randomized trial demonstrated that AI-guided erythropoiesis-stimulating agent dosing achieved outcomes comparable to physician-directed dosing. Technology-guided dry-weight adjustment is supported by a meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials. Machine learning for vascular access is evolving toward preoperative clinical decision support, while peritoneal dialysis is beginning to receive greater attention from the machine learning community. Large language models are entering nephrology along two complementary paths: open generative systems for education and clinical support, and deterministic, protocol-driven frameworks designed for safety-critical bedside applications. At the same time, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has released comprehensive lifecycle guidance for AI-enabled medical devices. The major challenge for AI in dialysis is no longer developing accurate prediction models. Instead, success will depend on effective workflow integration, validation across diverse patient populations, ongoing postdeployment monitoring, and demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient outcomes.

title: AI-Based Model for Predicting Type 2 Diabetes Risk Using Lifestyle Factors Among Senior Nursing Students
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Alexandria University; conditions: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 200; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study will develop and test an artificial intelligence (AI) model that estimates the risk of type 2 diabetes among senior (third- and fourth-year) nursing students at the Faculty of Nursing, Alexandria University, Egypt. Type 2 diabetes is common in Egypt, and many cases are not diagnosed. Daily habits such as diet, physical activity, and body weight play a major role in who develops it. Nursing students will become health care providers who teach patients about healthy living, so it is important to find those who may be at risk early. About 200 students will take part. Each student will complete a questionnaire about personal information and the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II, which measures health habits such as nutrition, physical activity, stress management, and health responsibility. The researcher will measure height, weight, waist size, and blood pressure. Each student's diabetes risk will be scored using the Arabic version of the Australian Type 2 Diabetes Risk Assessment Tool (AUSDRISK), which classifies risk as low, moderate, or high. These data will be used to build a machine learning model that predicts each student's diabetes risk level from lifestyle and body measurement factors, and shows which factors influenced the prediction most. Students will then try the model and rate how useful and easy to use it is. No treatment or intervention will be given. The study aims to support early identification of students at risk and to provide a model that nursing education programs and community health nurses could use in preventive health efforts.

title: Large language models are unstable as autonomous medical evaluators across clinical tasks.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated evaluators of medical text ("LLM-as-judge"). We tested whether LLM-evaluator performance validated on one medical task against a human reference standard remains stable on a structurally different task. We evaluated 10 LLMs (3 locally served open-source and 7 API models: Claude, GPT, DeepSeek) as autonomous judges on 3 tasks with human reference labels: LiveQA-Med answer quality (n = 300), PubMedQA research appraisal (n = 300), and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage on MIMIC-IV-Ext (n = 256). Each case was scored 3 times per model at temperature zero (25 680 judgments). Analyses used cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, quadratic-weighted Cohen's κ, and false-discovery-rate correction. Evaluator performance was unstable across tasks: no model ranked in the top 3 on all 3 tasks, and every model shifted by 3 or more rank positions between at least one pair of tasks. In the highest-stakes task, ESI level 1 (Resuscitation) cases were under-triaged in 89.1% of evaluations, in all 10 models (range 70.2%-96.9%). Best triage agreement only reached the human inter-rater range (Claude Opus quadratic-weighted κ = 0.60 [0.54, 0.66]). Locally served 7-27B models (no per-query charge) occupied the Pareto frontier on the text tasks but only its low-concordance end on triage. LLM-evaluator performance is unstable between medical tasks that differ in cognitive structure; performance validated on one task should not be assumed to transfer to another. Task-specific validation against human reference labels is required before deployment, and emergency triage demands human oversight at the highest-acuity tier.

title: Decoding Ewing sarcoma: from EWSR1::FLI1 translocation to advanced diagnostic approaches.
source: PubMed · Expert review of molecular diagnostics
desc: [Expert review of molecular diagnostics] This review discusses Ewing sarcoma and its diagnostic approaches, highlighting emerging high-throughput technologies that address current diagnostic limitations by enabling rapid, accurate, and personalized diagnostic strategies. Diagnostic approaches for Ewing sarcoma encompass conventional imaging modalities, including X-ray, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET), together with histopathological and molecular techniques such as Immunohistochemistry (IHC), Reverse Transcriptase-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR), Fluorescence in Situ Hybridization (FISH), as well as advanced modalities like liquid biopsy, Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), nano-diagnostic methods, and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven analytical tools. Together, these enable earlier and more accurate detection, molecular profiling, personalized medicine, and precision-guided clinical decision-making. Emerging diagnostic technologies offer new opportunities to improve the detection and molecular characterization of Ewing sarcoma through earlier diagnosis, comprehensive genomic profiling, and personalized medicine. Although NGS, liquid biopsy, and AI have demonstrated significant potential for precision diagnostics, their clinical implementation remains limited by high costs, restricted accessibility, and the need for standardized protocols and clinical validation. Continued technological refinement, integration into routine practice, and access will help overcome existing barriers, strengthen precision diagnostics, improve patient outcomes, and support personalized medicine.

title: Predicting Extubation Failure Using Machine Learning
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Universitas Indonesia; conditions: Extubation Failure, Critical Illness; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 1065; status: RECRUITING] The goal of this observational study is to predict who will have problems after the breathing tube is removed. Taking out the tube is called extubation, and having these problems is called extubation failure. Participants are adults in the intensive care unit (ICU) who use a breathing machine (ventilator). The main questions it aims to answer are: * How well can computer tools predict problems in the 7 days after the tube is removed? * Which information, such as age or blood tests, matters most for the prediction? Extubation failure means the participant needs the tube put back in, needs a surgical opening in the neck to help breathing, or dies. Researchers will use machine learning to build the computer tools. Machine learning is a type of artificial intelligence that finds patterns in data. Researchers will compare five types of machine learning to see which works best. They will build the tools with participants from Dr. Cipto Mangunkusumo National General Hospital in Jakarta. They will test the tools with participants from Universitas Indonesia Hospital in Depok. Participants get their usual care. Doctors do not use the tools to make treatment decisions. Researchers will: * Record health information about participants before the tube is removed * Follow participants for 7 days after the tube is removed

title: Machine Learning Based Detection of Chronic Kidney Disease using Full Blood Count from a Ghanaian Hospital Population with an Integrated Web Application
desc: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is usually silent until advanced, and the tests confirming it are frequently unaffordable in sub-Saharan Africa, whereas the full blood count (FBC) is inexpensive and widely performed. We assessed whether machine learning applied to the FBC can detect CKD, and how far its reported performance depends on where synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) is applied. Records of 155 patients at the Ho Technical University Hospital, Ghana, 43 (27.7%) with CKD, yielded ten features: age, cardiovascular disease and eight raw FBC parameters. Eleven algorithms, six resampling strategies and thirteen ensembles were compared under repeated stratified cross-validation. With SMOTE applied before the train-test split, the protocol under which the deployed models were fitted, Random Forest and Extra Trees both reached an accuracy of 83.9%, with sensitivities of 0.893 and 0.857 and areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.925 and 0.939; repeated cross-validation gave an accuracy of 0.809 {+/-} 0.051 and an AUC of 0.897. With resampling confined to the training folds, the same features gave a held-out accuracy of 61.5% and an AUC of 0.604 in 39 unseen patients. Age was the only variable separating the groups after correction for multiple testing (median 64 versus 47 years, adjusted p = 0.0026). The models are deployed as NephroScan GH (https://nephroscangh.com), which explains every prediction. The FBC carries a real but moderate signal for CKD, and the 22.4 point gap between the two protocols quantifies how far a single preprocessing decision can move a reported accuracy.

title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
desc: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. We also present head-to-head comparisons on these tasks with BLASTp, DIAMOND, RxnPred and Horizyn. Structure conditioning improves fingerprint similarity on homology-stratified splits, but a matched sequence-only ablation at the best configuration finds no measurable effect on exact recovery. Data coverage and chemical initialisation of the vocabulary seem to matter more than encoder geometry.

title: Applying artificial intelligence to optical coherence tomography for detection and subtyping of basal cell carcinoma.
source: PubMed · Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft = Journal of the German Society of Dermatology : JDDG
desc: [Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft = Journal of the German Society of Dermatology : JDDG] Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cancer and a major public health burden. Noninvasive techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) may reduce unnecessary biopsies and enable earlier detection. However, effective OCT interpretation requires expertise. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help overcome this barrier. An AI model based on a U-Net convolutional neural network was trained using 4,680 annotated OCT image frames from 39 BCCs, 5,640 frames from 47 premalignant and benign lesions, and 12,360 frames from 103 scans of healthy skin. Detection performance was evaluated on an independent test set comprising 26 scans (3,120 frames) from 16 BCCs, 5 premalignant lesions, and 5 benign lesions. External validation used independent clinical data from 25 histologically confirmed BCCs (18 nodular, 7 superficial). AI-assisted OCT generated visual overlays corresponding to established BCC features and identified tumor areas. In the independent test set, the area under the ROC curve was 95.5 % for nodular and 98.2 % for superficial BCC. In clinical validation, all BCCs were detected, and subtype concordance with histology was achieved in 21 of 25 cases (83 %). AI-assisted OCT shows potential to improve non-invasive BCC diagnostics and warrants further clinical evaluation.

title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
desc: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

title: Prototyping OSA: A New Framework for Predicting Cardiovascular Outcomes and CPAP Benefit
desc: RationaleObstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with major adverse cardiac events (MACE); continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) has not reduced MACE in randomized trials. We hypothesized that multidomain machine learning would identify OSA subgroups differing in cardiovascular risk and CPAP response. MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of SAVE trial data. After preprocessing, Gaussian mixture models were fitted; Bayesian information criterion and C-index selected five prototypes. Cox models estimated MACE risk by prototype. Baseline quality of life (EQoL), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), and Framingham Risk Score (FRS) were compared; an existing causal survival forest model estimated prototype-specific CPAP effects on cardiovascular risk. Measurements and Main ResultsAfter preprocessing, five OSA prototypes were identified among 2,676 participants using 88 baseline variables. Prototypes differed in selected demographic, cardiometabolic, medication, and sleep variables, including smoking status, diabetes, prior myocardial infarction/stroke, antiplatelet/lipid-lowering therapy, BMI, oxygenation metrics, apnea-hypopnea index, and ESS (overall p<0.001). They also differed in baseline EQoL, FRS, MACE rate, and predicted CPAP response. Prototype 1 had the highest ESS, FRS, and MACE rate, whereas Prototype 5 had the lowest FRS and MACE rate. Using the causal survival forest model to assess prototype-specific CPAP effects on cardiovascular risk, Prototype 5 was predicted to benefit from CPAP (p<0.05), whereas Prototypes 1, 3, and 4 showed no benefit or possible harm. ConclusionThese findings demonstrate heterogeneity in cardiovascular risk and predicted CPAP response, potentially explaining neutral trial results. After external validation, these prototypes could guide trial enrichment and targeted CPAP use to improve cardiovascular outcomes. Impact StatementThis study advances clinical medicine by identifying multidomain OSA prototypes that differ in baseline cardiovascular risk and predicted cardiovascular response to CPAP, potentially supporting more precise treatment selection and future cardiovascular-outcomes trials. It adds to the disease knowledge base by showing that OSA-related cardiovascular risk is not captured by conventional severity metrics alone, but reflects interactions among sleep, cardiometabolic, demographic, and clinical characteristics. title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
desc: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.
